 Follow Northern Lights Forecast: Here’s Where The Aurora Could Be Visible This Week
 Zachary Folk, Forbes Staff Updated Mon, November 16, 2026 at 6:11 PM UTC 2 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Topline
 The northern lights have a chance to be visible from some states near the U.S.-Canadian border on Tuesday night into Wednesday morning, according to a forecast from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, as experts expect geomagnetic storms caused by high speed solar winds.
 The aurora borealis could be visible from some northern states later this week.
 Key Facts
 NOAA is predicting a Kp index of four out of nine on Tuesday night, meaning the northern lights could appear brighter and visible farther from Earth's magnetic north pole than usual.
 Forecasters are predicting high speed solar winds from a coronal hole could reach Earth on Tuesday night and Wednesday morning, which could combine with a coronal mass ejection recorded on Saturday to create minor geomagnetic storm conditions.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement NOAA is only expecting minor storms, according to the most recent three-day forecast , but even minor storms can cause the aurora borealis to appear visible from the northern U.S.
 CONTRA
 The lights have a lower visibility chance on Monday night, with NOAA predicting a Kp index of three.
 Where Could the Northern Lights Be Visible?
 In many states along the U.S.-Canadian border on Tuesday night, according to NOAA's forecast map. These include northern Washington, northern Idaho, northern Montana, northern South Dakota and much of North Dakota. Some parts of the upper Midwest could also see the aurora, including the northern reaches of Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan's Upper Peninsula. Most of Alaska also has a chance to see the aurora Tuesday night, with a large portion of the state's interior having a high chance, according to NOAA.
 What's the Best Way to View the Northern Lights?
 Experts at NOAA suggest prospective viewers travel toward Earth's magnetic north pole. Viewers should then search for an ideal vantage point, ideally a hill or mountain with a clear view of the sky facing north and far away from cities or other bright light sources. The aurora is typically most active in the hours just before and after midnight, so viewers should plan to watch the skies between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m.
 What's the Best Way to Photograph the Northern Lights?
 Smartphones are capable of capturing quality photographs of the northern lights, an expert who spoke to National Geographic said, provided photographers use the correct equipment and settings. Users should remember to turn off flash and use their device's night mode while shooting. If possible, take photos using the RAW image format. Photographers should also remember to bring a timer and tripod for their devices, as cameras held still for longer periods of time in the low-light conditions are better suited for capturing the aurora.
